source: Poddar, Sahoo, Ghosh (2025) Understanding Syllogistic Reasoning in LLMs from Formal and Natural Language Perspectives
finding: Fourteen models were tested on 160 syllogisms (40 base items with variants), split into congruent (logic and belief agree) and incongruent (they conflict). Strong recent models show almost no belief bias. Weak and mid models show a lot. Two models show the reverse sign.
numbers: Bias = accuracy congruent minus incongruent, pooled over 4 prompt strategies x 3 temperatures. Gemini 2.5 Flash 100.0/99.2 (+0.9); Gemini 2.5 Pro 100.0/98.6 (+1.4); GPT-OSS-20B 99.2/98.4 (+0.8); GLM-4.6 99.4/97.5 (+1.9); Kimi-K2 99.6/92.1 (+7.5); DeepSeek V3.1 99.7/91.8 (+7.9); Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite 95.0/82.5 (+12.5); Llama 3.1 8B +12.9; Qwen3-Next 80B Thinking 86.3/58.3 (+28.0); Llama 3.3 70B 85.3/53.6 (+31.6); Llama 3.2 3B 82.0/35.2 (+46.9); Qwen3-Next Instruct -7.9; Gemma 3 27B -13.7. Mean +10.81 pp (SD 16.32), t13=2.47, p=.028, Cohen d=0.66; 12 of 14 positive. Bias falls as general ability rises (rho=-0.565, p=.035).
quote: Twelve of 14 models exhibit positive belief bias
limits: Accuracy differences, not d-prime or criterion, so bias and sensitivity are mixed. Frontier models sit at the ceiling (about 99%), so a gap cannot show. Only 160 items, 40 base. Strategies pooled, so plain versus CoT is not isolated. Preprint, not peer reviewed. No Claude or GPT-4/5 models in this table.
agent_relevance: For a strong current model on easy categorical syllogisms the belief gap is small (about 1 to 8 pp). Do not expect it to show on easy items. Test on hard, multi-model items and under load, where the ceiling does not hide it.

source: Poddar, Sahoo, Ghosh (2025) Understanding Syllogistic Reasoning in LLMs (strategy effects)
finding: Prompting strategy (zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot with a belief-bias trap, zero-shot CoT) did not help in a consistent way. Few-shot was worst. Temperature did nothing once majority voting was used. The same top models that ace validity score near chance when asked if the conclusion is believable.
numbers: Few-shot mean accuracy 79.1% vs zero-shot 82.7%: paired t41=2.50, p=.0165, Holm p=.0495, d=-0.39. Friedman across 4 strategies chi2=3.24, p=.356 (no overall effect). Wilcoxon p=.0584 after correction. Syntax accuracy 81.7% vs believability (NLU) accuracy 56.2%; Gemini 2.5 Flash 99.6 syntax vs 51.7 NLU. 26,880 evaluations in all.
limits: Answer format forced to one word, so zero-shot CoT may not reason before answering in the same way as free CoT. No token counts. Per-model strategy results are not in the text I read.
agent_relevance: A belief-trap few-shot example did not reduce bias and may hurt. Do not assume extra prompt scaffolding is free. Measure it per model.

source: Noe et al. (2025/2026, LREC) BIS Reasoning 1.0: Japanese Benchmark for Belief-Inconsistent Syllogistic Reasoning
finding: All items are logically valid but conclude something false in the real world. Accuracy is the share accepted as valid. Modern reasoning models are near perfect. Older chat models and Claude-3 models reject many valid-unbelievable items. Reasoning effort is the lever for one model.
numbers: Basic zero-shot prompt, Japanese. BIS Reasoning 1.0 / NeuBAROCO accuracy: GPT-5-mini (medium effort) 99.72/91.92; GPT-5-nano (medium) 98.84/91.32; gpt-oss-20b 98.56/89.52; Qwen3-32B no-think 99.58/94.01, think 99.12/97.60; GPT-4o 79.54/94.01; GPT-4-turbo 59.48/67.66; GPT-5-nano minimum effort 69.22/73.05; Claude-3-sonnet-20240229 20.34/78.44; Claude-3-opus-20240229 7.18/61.07.
limits: Valid-only items: there are no invalid items, so a model that says 'valid' to everything scores 100. Accuracy cannot separate sensitivity from response bias. A low score may be over-rejection, a criterion shift. Japanese prompts, one prompt per model. Claude-3 models are deprecated and old, not current. Full GPT-5 not in the table I read. Model versions and effort settings differ across rows.
agent_relevance: Shows the valid-unbelievable corner is the hard one for older models, and that reasoning effort moved GPT-5-nano from 69.2 to 98.8. Our test set must include invalid-believable and invalid-unbelievable items, or we cannot tell skill from a lean to 'valid'.

source: Noe et al. (2025/2026) BIS Reasoning 1.0, GPT-4o error re-evaluation with different prompts
finding: The authors took 100 belief-inconsistent items GPT-4o had failed and re-asked them with different prompts. An explicit step-by-step prompt rescued most. A prompt that warned about belief conflict rescued many. Plain or casual prompts rescued almost none.
numbers: Of 100 prior failures (English-prompt retest): CoT prompt 87% now correct; focus_logic prompt (mentions belief inconsistency, urges strict logic) 76%; polite prompt about 65%; basic 3%; casual 5%.
limits: Items were chosen because GPT-4o failed them once. Re-asking a failed item can succeed by chance, and the basic-prompt result (3%) is the only control. Valid-only items, so a 'say valid more' lean also scores. Only GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: A warning that belief and logic may conflict, plus step-by-step reasoning, rescued most prior failures of an older model. This supports a cheap conflict warning plus a reasoning step. It does not show equal-token efficiency.

source: Clark, Dalvi Mishra, Tafjord (2023/2024) BaRDa: A Belief and Reasoning Dataset that Separates Factual Accuracy and Reasoning Ability
finding: Entailments (2 premises, 1 hypothesis) were built with true or false facts and valid or invalid entailment, 3000 items. GPT-4 judged invalid entailments much worse when the facts were true (believable) than when false. Valid entailments showed a smaller shift the other way. That is the classic belief-bias shape in 2023 GPT-4.
numbers: Reasoning accuracy by type (columns FF, TF, FT, TT = facts true/false then entailment valid/invalid; order read from a garbled table and checked against the GPT3c row): GPT-4 FF 90.0, TF 42.1, FT 75.2, TT 92.1. GPT-3.5 84.5/31.1/58.1/90.4. Overall GPT-4 reasoning accuracy 79.2%, factual accuracy 87.1%. My d-prime from GPT-4 rates: believable (true facts) hit .921, false alarm .579, d'=1.21, criterion c=-0.81; unbelievable (false facts) hit .752, false alarm .100, d'=1.96, c=+0.30. GPT-3.5: d' 0.81 vs 1.22, c -0.90 vs +0.41. Cell counts: FF 672, TF 541, FT 609, TT 1178.
limits: The d-prime and criterion are my own calculation from table cells, not the authors'. Cell counts are unequal. 'Believable' here means the facts are true, not a rated conclusion believability. Entailment-style, not categorical syllogisms. GPT-4 from 2023, not current. Table layout garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Best available SDT-style number for a strong model: d' fell from 1.96 to 1.21 and the criterion moved about 1.1 z-units toward 'valid' when content was believable. This is a template for scoring our agent: per-cell hit and false-alarm rates, then d' and c.

source: Macchi et al. (2019) How to Get Rid of the Belief Bias: Boosting Analytical Thinking via Pragmatics, Table 1 and review of earlier instruction studies
finding: Macchi's Table 1 lists earlier numbers for correct responses on valid-believable and invalid-believable items: Evans et al. 1983 92% and 8%; Newstead et al. 1992 Exp 5 75% and 83%; Evans et al. 1994 81% and 56%. So the 1983 invalid-believable correct rate is printed as 8% (92% accepted), not 29% (71% accepted). The long-instruction effect of Newstead Exp 5 was only partly replicated by Evans 1994.
numbers: Evans 1983: VB 92%, IB correct 8%. Newstead 1992 Exp 5: VB 75%, IB correct 83%, control rejection of IB about 50%. Evans 1994 (same instructions): VB 81%, IB correct 56%. Macchi 2019 single item, N=130: VB 94% (untrained) 96% (trained); IB correct 4% and 10%.
quote: an attempt to replicate the results (Evans et al., 1994) was less successful
limits: Macchi cites these from the originals; I did not see the 1983, 1992 or 1994 papers. The 92/8 pair matches Trippas 2018 Table 1 (.92/.08) and a Futility Closet summary (92% believable, 46% valid-unbelievable, 8% invalid-unbelievable), but not the Wikipedia/ResearchGate 89/71/56/10 set. They may come from different experiments or pooling. Not resolved.
agent_relevance: Two sets of figures for the classic acceptance rates both appear in secondary text. Quote ranges, not a single number, in design notes. Long, explicit logic instructions can help a lot but gains vary by replication (83% vs 56%).

source: Macchi et al. (2019) Experiment 2 and review of attempts to fix belief bias by instruction
finding: Macchi states that earlier attempts to cut belief bias by stressing that only necessary conclusions should be accepted (Barston 1986; Evans, Handley and Harper 2001; Handley, Newstead and Trippas 2011) were not successful. Her own wording worked on one item in Exp 2: 'necessarily' wording gave 66% and 77% correct rejections of the invalid-believable item, against 4% and 10% in the control.
numbers: Exp 2, correct on the invalid-believable item. Necessarily: 66% untrained, 77% trained (N=82; difference p=.45). Criteria-of-logic: 41% untrained, 67% trained (N=80; chi2=4.91, p=.03). Necessarily vs criteria, untrained: chi2(N=101)=6.25, p=.017; trained p=.39. Control vs necessarily: untrained chi2(N=101)=42.24, trained chi2(N=111)=47.91, both p<.001. Control vs criteria: untrained 19.84 (N=100), trained 36.92 (N=110).
limits: The 'not successful' statement is Macchi's summary, not my reading of those three papers. One syllogism per condition, so this is a demonstration, not a rate. Her wording added a pragmatic framing and a 'Why?' question, so it differs from earlier 'must be true' wordings. Different participants per condition.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open: the wording effect is one-item evidence, and older multi-item wording studies reportedly failed. For an LLM, test several wordings across many items before building a prompt rule on 'necessarily follows'.

source: Newstead, Pollard, Evans, Allen (1992) The source of belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning. Cognition 45, 257-284 (abstract seen in a search result summary)
finding: Experiments 1 and 2 used only determinate syllogisms (conclusions that follow or are contradicted). With those, the logic-by-belief interaction disappeared. The authors read this as support for misinterpreted necessity, then found support for a mental-models account in Experiments 3 to 5.
numbers: Not read. No cell values seen. Exp 5 numbers come via Macchi (d06).
limits: Abstract level only, via a search summary, not the paper. A later check of whether the interaction vanishes in other labs was not done.
agent_relevance: Human version of gap 4: bias is concentrated in indeterminate invalid items. A counterexample search should help most there. Build the LLM test with both determinate and indeterminate invalid items.

source: Evans, Handley, Harper (2001) Necessity, possibility and belief: a study of syllogistic reasoning. QJEP-A 54, 935-958 (abstract seen in a search result summary)
finding: Three experiments asked for 'necessarily follows' and 'possibly follows' judgments. People rejected unbelievable conclusions more than abstract controls under both instructions and across all syllogism types. There was also positive belief bias and an interaction between belief and logical form.
numbers: Not read. No effect sizes seen.
limits: Abstract level only. Macchi (d07) says this paper's necessity emphasis did not remove belief bias.
agent_relevance: Necessity versus possibility wording has been tested across several syllogism types in humans, so a wording test on LLMs has a template.

source: Akinfaderin, Diallo (2026) FregeLogic at SemEval-2026 Task 11 (prompt strategies and fusion results)
finding: On 960 syllogisms balanced across the four cells, open-weight models (Llama 4 Maverick, Scout, Qwen3-32B) differed in content effect more than in accuracy. Chain-of-thought did not uniformly cut the content effect. Simple CoT had the lowest average CE; few-shot CoT raised CE for Maverick.
numbers: Accuracy 79.5 to 89.0% across 12 model-prompt combos, content effect (CE) 3.49 to 13.71. Simple CoT mean CE 5.24 (lowest). Maverick few-shot CE 3.83 vs few-shot CoT 10.11. Pure 5-model ensemble 93.4% accuracy, CE 3.39; cell accuracy VB 95.9, VU 96.0, IB 90.2, IU 91.9. Score = Accuracy/(1+ln(1+CE)). Cells: VB 240, VU 240, IB 234, IU 246.
limits: Open-weight models, not frontier. Prompts and models chosen by nested CV on the same 960 items, no held-out test. CE is the shared-task metric (average accuracy differences), not d-prime. Tokens not matched across prompts.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: CoT did not reliably reduce the content effect for strong open models; the effect depends on model and prompt. Equal-token comparisons are still missing.

source: Akinfaderin, Diallo (2026) FregeLogic: disagreement-routed Z3 verification
finding: Z3 was called only when the 5-LLM ensemble split 3-2. This selective check beat both the ensemble alone and using Z3 on more cases. Splits were rare. Z3 overrode the majority 30 times: 19 right, 11 wrong; all wrong flips falsely rejected a valid syllogism because the LLM extracted the structure wrongly.
numbers: 3-2 splits: 76 of 960 (7.9%). Tiebreaker: accuracy 94.3+-0.9, CE 2.85, combined 41.88 vs pure ensemble 93.4, 3.39, 39.12 (CE down 16%, accuracy up 0.9). Z3 on 4-1 splits too (confidence+Z3): 91.7%, CE 6.15, score 31.77. Z3 veto: 74.1%, CE 26.70. Net gain 8 items over 5 folds. Invalid-believable accuracy 90.2 to 94.5. Scout in the minority on 53.9% of splits (41 of 76); Maverick few-shot 28.9% (22 of 76). Cost: 6 LLM calls, about 4,300 tokens and 12.1 s sequential per item.
limits: The trigger is ensemble disagreement, not the model's belief about the conclusion, so this is not the conflict flag of gap 9. Gain is small (8 items) and standard deviations overlap (41.88+-5.97 vs 39.12+-5.37). Settings tuned on the same data. Unanimous wrong ensembles (strong belief) are not rescued.
agent_relevance: Supports routing extra verification only to uncertain items and not trusting a checker everywhere. But there is no equal-token comparison against spending the same tokens on verifying all items, so gap 5 is not closed.

source: Akinfaderin, Diallo (2026) FregeLogic: Z3-only baseline
finding: Using the SMT solver alone on LLM-extracted structure was worse than prompting. It over-predicts invalid because extraction errors break valid chains.
numbers: Z3 only: accuracy 74.7+-2.0, CE 26.28; cell accuracy VB 50.5, VU 53.9, IB 98.0, IU 97.2. Structured-output calls cut Z3 failure rates from about 22% to near zero. Extraction failure by cell 0.0% (VB, IB, IU) and 0.4% (VU, 1 of 241).
limits: Extraction by Llama or Qwen open models; stronger extractors may close the gap.
agent_relevance: Formalise-and-prove is only as good as the translation. A prover adds an invalid lean that must be checked. Never let a checker veto high-agreement answers.

source: Kartac et al. (2026) UFAL-CUNI at SemEval-2026 Task 11: modular neuro-symbolic method (ablation table)
finding: With the same small reasoning model (Qwen3 4B Thinking), translating to first-order logic and running Prover9 beat direct end-to-end prompting on accuracy and content effect. Using the same model as the prover on the translated formulas was worse than the real prover.
numbers: Subtask 1: full pipeline accuracy 95.83, CE 2.28, CS 45.61; single-step parsing 95.81, CE 2.14; parse directly to Prover9 syntax 85.97, CE 12.23; LLM instead of prover 79.22, CE 20.21; end-to-end zero-shot 84.17, CE 14.67, CS 11.25. 18% of formulas had syntax errors in the direct-to-Prover9 ablation. The 4B model beat the 30B-A3B in accuracy.
limits: Small 4B model; a frontier model's end-to-end score would be higher (see d14). No token counts. Dataset has label errors (10 of 21 validation errors were wrong labels).
agent_relevance: For weak or mid models, prover beats prompt. A rule-based transpiler step matters more than model size. Still not an equal-token test (gap 6 open).

source: Muhamad et al. (2026) ITLC at SemEval-2026 Task 11: Normalization and Deterministic Parsing for Formal Reasoning in LLMs
finding: An LLM (gemini-3-flash-preview) rewrote each argument into a canonical syllogism form and a deterministic parser decided validity. This got perfect English validity accuracy with zero measured content effect. The LLM-only baseline was already very high. A formal first-order-logic rewrite and a predicate-argument rewrite were worse than the canonical syllogism notation.
numbers: Normalisation comparison (English validity): raw data 92.10 acc / bias 10.63; predicate-argument 77.48 / 8.17; FOL 96.85 / 3.19; syllogism notation 98.95 / 2.13. Final: LLM-only 98.43 acc, bias 2.13; Norm+Parsing 100 / 0.0. Multilingual validity: LLM-only 96.87 / 4.16; Norm+Parsing 96.88 / 3.12; with English-pivot translation 100 / 0.0. Relevance task: LLM-only 95.78 acc, bias 5.0.
limits: Test set about 190 items; the paper lists four LLM-only mismatches (the 98.43% figure and the count do not match exactly): 2 false positives with plausibility lean, 2 on partitive quantifiers). 'Bias' is the shared-task content-effect score. Prompt cost not reported; the pipeline needs extra LLM calls. The parser handles only standard categorical forms.
agent_relevance: For a strong current model on standard syllogisms the plain prompt already leaves only a few percent content effect, so the gain from a normaliser or prover is small and costs extra calls. Predicate-argument abstraction was worse than staying near natural syllogism form: abstraction is not automatically good.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning by Combining Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers
finding: LINC translates premises to FOL and calls Prover9. It gave large gains on ProofWriter but only matched CoT for GPT-4 on FOLIO. The two methods fail on different items. One frequent CoT error is the converse fallacy, the same fallacy that belief bias exploits.
numbers: GPT-4 on FOLIO: CoT 75.3% vs LINC 72.5% average accuracy; LINC about 26% higher than CoT on ProofWriter (abstract). FOL syntax errors: GPT-4 13%, GPT-3.5 24%, StarCoder+ 38%. Predicts Uncertain 57% (LINC) vs 41% (CoT). Precision on True/False: LINC 93% vs CoT 81%; recall 60% vs 75%. Of 74 FOLIO items with at least one error, only 21 were shared. Error similarity LINC vs others 0.14 to 0.22, versus 0.52 to 0.56 among prompting methods.
limits: FOLIO and ProofWriter, not syllogism belief tests. Translation is lossy: implicit knowledge is lost so LINC says Uncertain. No token accounting in the text I read; the paper notes reliance on costly API calls.
agent_relevance: A prover helps most when it fails differently from the model, so combine, do not replace. Lost implicit knowledge (for example 'Harry is a person') is the failure mode: it makes valid items look non-entailed.

source: Ryu et al. (2025, ICLR) CLOVER: Compositional First-Order Logic Translation and Verification for Complex Logical Reasoning, inference cost table
finding: The only cost number I found for solver pipelines. API cost on a subset of AR-LSAT with gpt-4o-mini rises with the amount of translation and verification.
numbers: Cost in USD: Standard 0.02; CoT 0.02; Logic-LM 0.08; SymbCoT 0.15; CLOVER 0.30 (row order from the raw text extraction of the table).
limits: AR-LSAT analytic reasoning, one cheap model, dollars not tokens, no accuracy-per-token curve. Not a belief-bias task.
agent_relevance: Solver pipelines cost 4x to 15x more than CoT on this set. Any equal-token comparison must give prompting the same budget, for example self-consistency voting.

source: Trippas, Thompson, Handley (2017) When fast logic meets slow belief (Discussion section re-read this session)
finding: The authors present their data as support for a parallel-processing model and against the strict default-interventionist claim that a fast belief answer pre-empts slow logic (the idea behind Evans and Curtis-Holmes 2005). Belief responses were faster only in the harder Experiment 2. Validity interfered with belief judgments even on complex problems.
numbers: Interference depends on problem complexity: modus ponens, belief judgments less accurate than validity judgments; modus tollens and single-model syllogisms, symmetrical interference; three-term multiple-model syllogisms, belief interferes more with validity. Effect sizes are in a22, a23 and b14.
limits: A reinterpretation by authors with a different theory, not a direct replication of the 10-second deadline. Within-participant design may add response competition (authors discuss it).
agent_relevance: No direct failed replication of the time-pressure effect was found. The claim that belief is always faster is contested. A short token budget for an LLM is an untested analog; test it rather than assume.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2025/2026) How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility (model list and scope, re-read this session)
finding: The 2025 positive result for CoT and steering was run on ten open models from three families only (Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Gemma-3), on 1,280 syllogisms covering all 64 syllogism types with binary plausible and implausible conclusions. Plausibility was treated as binary, not graded.
numbers: 1,280 syllogisms; 70-30 train-test split for the probes and steering. No proprietary or frontier model in the evaluation.
limits: Scope statement only. Detailed CE numbers are in c14 and c15.
agent_relevance: Confirms gaps 2 and 10: no frontier-model CoT evidence in this line of work and no graded-belief analysis.

source: Maraia, Valentino, Zanzotto, Ranaldi (2026) Abstract Activation Spaces for Content-Invariant Reasoning in LLMs (abstract and introduction)
finding: The authors state that the content effect persists even when models write step-by-step explanations, and that earlier abstraction-by-prompt and steering approaches do not reliably suppress it. They propose a learned activation-space method that needs model internals.
numbers: Abstract and introduction only; plotted values were garbled in extraction and are not used.
limits: A statement from the abstract of a paper whose method needs access to activations, so it does not apply to a prompt-only scaffold. Authors overlap with the steering line of work.
agent_relevance: Another claim that CoT rationales can inherit the semantic shortcut. Supports checking the final verdict against an independent abstracted run instead of trusting one rationale.

source: Howarth (2015) Believe it or not: examining the case for intuitive logic and effortful beliefs (University of Plymouth thesis; repository abstract page)
finding: Several experiments with a secondary task found belief-based judgments made more errors, validity interfered with belief judgments, and logic judgments were sometimes slower. This cuts against the simple claim that belief is always the fast default.
numbers: Not read; the PDF could not be downloaded.
limits: Abstract only, paraphrased by a summarising tool. Single thesis.
agent_relevance: More evidence that the time-pressure story is not simple (gap 8): no strong replication of Evans and Curtis-Holmes as stated, plus results that cut against it.

source: Evans, Barston, Pollard (1983) On the conflict between logic and belief in syllogistic reasoning, Experiment 1
finding: Primary paper obtained and read in full text. Experiment 1 gives the famous cell values: believable conclusions were accepted about equally often whether valid or not, unbelievable ones were accepted much less, and mostly when valid.
numbers: Exp 1, N=24 undergraduates, 4 problems each (one per cell), prose passages, only E and I premises, retrospective verbal protocols. Percent accepting: valid-believable 92, valid-unbelievable 46, invalid-believable 92, invalid-unbelievable 8. Correct when logic agrees with belief 92%, when it conflicts 27%. Instruction already said the conclusion must 'necessarily follow'.
quote: belief bias was more marked on invalid than on valid syllogisms
limits: One problem per cell per person; 24 people. The interaction is read from cell means; the paper gives no effect size.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 8 for Exp 1: 92/46/92/8 is the real Exp 1 set, N=24. Invalid-believable acceptance was 92% even with 'necessarily follows' wording.

source: Evans, Barston, Pollard (1983) Experiment 2 (N=64, four groups)
finding: Replicated and extended Exp 1. The belief effect did not come from putting premises inside a prose passage, and did not depend on being asked to explain answers. Belief, logic and their interaction were all significant.
numbers: N=64, 16 per group (prose+retrospective protocol; premises only; prose+think-aloud; prose, no protocol). Pooled percent accepting: valid-believable 86, valid-unbelievable 62, invalid-believable 66, invalid-unbelievable 13 (A-C conclusions only: 88/56/72/13; C-A: 84/68/59/13). Binomial tests: belief p<.001, validity p<.001, interaction p<.01. Correct 87% when logic agrees with belief, 48% when it conflicts. Group differences not significant (four 2x4 chi-squares).
limits: Cell values read from a pdftotext layout; row labels are scrambled in the extraction but the means agree arithmetically with the group rows.
agent_relevance: Wikipedia's 89/56/71/10 matches no cell exactly; the nearest is the A-C row here (88/56/72/13). Invalid-believable acceptance across Exp 1-3 is 66-92%.

source: Evans, Barston, Pollard (1983) Experiment 3 (N=32, stronger necessity instruction)
finding: Instruction was reworded to stress logical necessity (answer yes if and only if the conclusion logically follows), repeated at the end. Belief bias stayed large. Invalid-believable acceptance was 67%, against 92% in Exp 1 and 66% in Exp 2, so wording did not remove it. The interaction fell just short of significance.
numbers: N=32, 8 problems each, think-aloud. Percent accepting pooled over Figure 2 and 3: valid-believable 91, valid-unbelievable 53, invalid-believable 67, invalid-unbelievable 6 (Fig 2: 91/53/69/3; Fig 3: 91/53/66/9). Interaction p=.067 one-tailed binomial. Correct 97% when logic agrees with belief, 43% when it conflicts. No Fig 2 vs Fig 3 difference.
quote: If they are 'failing to accept the logical task,' it is because they are unable to do so.
limits: Cross-experiment comparison of instruction effects is confounded (different N, items, designs). The authors suggest the weaker interaction may come from the changed instructions.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: necessity-emphasis wording alone did not remove the bias in the original data. That fits the view that Macchi's 4% to 66% is a single-item demonstration. Test on many items before relying on it.

source: Evans, Barston, Pollard (1983) General discussion and protocol analysis (selective scrutiny and misinterpreted necessity, first proposed)
finding: The original authors offered both later theories. (1) Selective scrutiny: people accept conclusions they agree with and check the logic more when they disagree. (2) Misinterpreted necessity: an invalid-believable conclusion is not contradicted by the premises, so people feel justified to favour belief. Protocols: people who accepted valid-unbelievable conclusions cited the premises more and irrelevant information less.
numbers: Exp 2 valid-unbelievable protocol chi-squares: more premise references X2=24.61, p<.001; fewer irrelevant references X2=15.11, p<.001. Exp 1 Fisher exact p=.026 (irrelevant references). Only 6 of 64 in Exp 2 accepted invalid-unbelievable conclusions against both logic and belief.
limits: Verbal protocols may be rationalisations. The data did not separate the two explanations.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4-6 are the engineering versions of these two hypotheses. The original paper does not decide between them, so only an LLM test can.

source: Ozeki et al. (2024) Exploring Reasoning Biases in LLMs Through Syllogism: NeuBAROCO
finding: English and Japanese syllogism sets tagged symbolic, congruent or incongruent. GPT-4 showed no clear drop on incongruent items in multiple choice; GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 70B dropped sharply. On the harder NLI task all models lost accuracy on incongruent items, GPT-4 too.
numbers: Multiple choice (80 items, English): GPT-4 overall 83.75, symbolic 75.00, congruent 90.00, incongruent 80.00; GPT-3.5 53.75/45.00/72.50/25.00; Llama-2-70B 56.25/65.00/62.50/35.00. Japanese GPT-4 95.00/85.00/97.50/100.00. Human (N=440, Shikishima 2009) 53.0/49.1/51.2/59.7. NLI (790 items): English GPT-4 77.47 overall, 82.92 congruent vs 67.23 incongruent; Japanese few-shot GPT-4 81.44 vs 73.95. Translate-and-Explain (90 items), English GPT-4: explanation only 77.78, with predicate-logic translation 96.67.
limits: gpt-4-0613 and gpt-3.5-1106 only. Multiple choice never has a 'none follows' answer, so it hides the invalid-lean bias. Accuracy gaps, not d-prime. 20 items per cell in multiple choice.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 side evidence: a strong 2023 model shows a 10-15 point drop on incongruent NLI items but not on easy multiple choice, so answer format decides whether the bias shows. A predicate-logic translation written inside the same prompt lifted GPT-4 from 77.78 to 96.67 (gap 7, prompt-only formalisation).

source: Evans, Handley, Bacon (2009) Reasoning under time pressure: a study of causal conditional inference
finding: Boundary condition for the time-pressure story. With conditional inference, speeding people up cut the number of inferences drawn but did not change the size of the belief bias, unlike the syllogism result. Belief effects also survived the instruction to assume the premises true.
numbers: Two experiments; participant numbers not on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract record only, summarised by a fetch tool; conditional inference, not syllogisms; not a replication of the 10 s syllogism deadline.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the time-pressure effect on belief bias is task-specific. Do not assume a short reasoning budget always raises belief bias in our agent; measure it.

source: Trippas, Handley, Verde (2013) The SDT model of belief bias: Complexity, time, and cognitive ability mediate the effects of believability
finding: With ROC analysis, believability changed accuracy on complex syllogisms but not simple ones in Exp 1. In Exp 2 this accuracy effect disappeared under time pressure and in people with lower cognitive capacity. So the accuracy cost of belief shows up when there is time and ability to use a reasoning strategy.
numbers: Two experiments; sample sizes not on the page.
limits: Abstract record only. Same SDT group as the 2018 meta-analysis. Cuts against, not for, the idea that time pressure harms reasoning through belief.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: an SDT-lens contradiction to the raw-rate reading of Evans and Curtis-Holmes. Deadlines may shift the criterion, not the accuracy. Score d-prime and criterion separately when changing budget.

source: Kim, Valentino, Freitas et al. (2025) Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
finding: Circuit-level study of syllogism completion in small models (GPT-2 sizes, Qwen2.5 0.5B and 1.5B, Llama 3.2 1B). Finds a middle-term suppression circuit and asks how belief bias contaminates it. A mechanism paper, not a behavioural measurement.
numbers: Only models with downstream accuracy of about 60% or more were analysed. Table 3 rows such as Qwen2.5-0.5B 1.00/0.96/0.90 were not decoded (column meaning unchecked).
limits: Abstract and fragments of a layout-scrambled PDF read. Small models; a completion task, not validity judgement.
agent_relevance: Low. Agrees with the steering result that plausibility and validity are entangled inside models; nothing usable at prompt level.

source: HABIB_TAZ at SemEval-2026 Task 11 (2026), baseline and ablation tables
finding: A fine-tuned encoder with plain cross-entropy already reaches near-ceiling validity accuracy with a small content effect. Extra regularisation moves the content effect by a few tenths of a point and the ranking score by many points.
numbers: Table 2 as printed: vanilla 98.95 acc, TCE 2.13, rank score 45.99; best FreeLB+MSE+DRO+Bias 99.47 acc, TCE 1.06, rank score 57.53; DRO+Bias 97.89, TCE 4.26. Some subtask rows print 100.0 and TCE 0.0. Blind test 191 items.
limits: Trained on the 960 task training syllogisms, so a supervised remedy, not a prompt. Layout-garbled table. Ranking score is noisy at ceiling.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 6: at 99% accuracy the content effect is 1-4 points and metric noise dominates; testing our agent needs hard items and d-prime, not these sets.

source: Search log for gaps 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 10 (WebSearch, arXiv API, OpenAlex, 2026-10-21)
finding: Repeated searches for a d-prime or criterion analysis of Claude, GPT-5 or o-series models on belief-bias syllogisms, for token-matched chain-of-thought comparisons, for verify-only-conflicts designs, for conflict-flag routing and for graded belief strength in LLMs returned nothing new. The 14-model accuracy-gap study (2512.12620) and BIS Reasoning remain the newest frontier-model sources.
numbers: arXiv queries combining belief bias, syllogism, Claude, reasoning effort, signal detection returned no relevant new paper. Newstead 1992, Evans 2001 and Evans and Curtis-Holmes 2005 have no open PDF in OpenAlex.
limits: Absence of search hits is not proof of absence. The search tool is US-only and returns few results per query.
